title: Structures
description: Defining structs, initializing them, arrays and nesting of structures, and pointers to structures.
objectives: Use arrays of structures and nested structures
Access struct members through a pointer with the arrow operator

content.heading: Defining and Initializing Structures
content.body: A struct groups related, possibly differently-typed fields (members) together under one name: struct Point { int x; int y; };. A variable is declared as struct Point p; (the struct keyword is required in plain C, unlike C++, unless a typedef is used — see the Enums and typedef lesson) and initialized either with a brace list, struct Point p = {3, 4};, or field-by-field, p.x = 3; p.y = 4;. Members are accessed with the dot operator: p.x. Structures make it possible to bundle logically-related data into one unit and pass it around as a single value, instead of tracking many loose, related variables individually.

content.heading: Arrays of Structures, Nesting, and Pointers to Structures
content.body:
struct Point points[3]; declares an array of 3 Point structures, each accessed and initialized like any array element: points[0].x = 1;. Structures can nest: struct Line { struct Point start; struct Point end; }; — accessing a nested field chains the dot operator, line.start.x.

When working with a pointer to a struct (struct Point *p = &point;), accessing a member requires either explicit dereferencing plus dot, (*p).x, or — far more commonly — the arrow operator, p->x, which combines dereferencing and member access in one step and is considered idiomatic C. Passing a large struct to a function by value copies the entire struct (potentially expensive for large structs); passing a pointer to it avoids that copy and, if desired, lets the function modify the caller's original struct directly.

content.explanation: printPoint takes a pointer (avoiding a struct copy) and uses -> to access members through it. const struct Point * documents that the function only reads the struct, never modifies it.

keyPoints: struct groups related fields under one name, accessed with the dot operator
An array of structures and nested structures both use ordinary array/dot-operator syntax, chained as needed
Access members through a struct pointer with -> (equivalent to, but cleaner than, (*p).member)
Passing a pointer to a struct avoids copying it and can allow in-place modification
commonMistakes: Using . instead of -> when accessing a member through a struct pointer (a compile error)
Passing a large struct by value where a pointer would avoid an unnecessary, potentially expensive copy
Forgetting the struct keyword when declaring a variable, without a typedef alias in place
